properties.notes: Victoriola functioned as a mutatio on the Via Aemilia between Ad Medias and Mutina, its diminutive name meaning 'little victory.' The Itinerarium Burdigalense placed it eight Roman miles beyond Ad Medias and three miles short of Mutina. No archaeological site has been securely matched to the station, though it likely stood near modern San Damaso on Modena's eastern approach.

properties.name: Mutina
properties.notes: Mutina appeared in both the Antonine Itinerary and the Itinerarium Burdigalense as a civitas on the Via Aemilia, twenty-five Roman miles beyond Bononia by the Antonine reckoning. The town gave its name to the Mutina campaign of 43 BCE, fought along this road when Mark Antony besieged Decimus Brutus inside its walls. Both itineraries used it as a fixed waypoint for the continuing stretch toward Regium Lepidi.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Pons Secies
properties.notes: Pons Secies, 'the bridge of the Secia,' marked the Via Aemilia's crossing of the river the Romans called the Secia, identified with the modern Secchia. The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it as a mutatio seven Roman miles out of Mutina on the way to Regium Lepidi. The crossing point corresponds closely to modern Rubiera, where the Via Emilia still bridges the Secchia, though the ancient bridge itself has not been excavated.

properties.name: Regium Lepidi
properties.notes: Regium Lepidi took its name from Marcus Aemilius Lepidus, the same consul who built the Via Aemilia, and stood as a civitas on the road on the stretch beyond Mutina according to the Antonine Itinerary. The Itinerarium Burdigalense listed it under the shortened name Regio on the same stretch of the pilgrim route to Placentia. Modern Reggio Emilia's street plan still traces the Roman layout along the ancient road.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Tannetum
properties.notes: Tannetum stood on the Via Aemilia between Regium Lepidi and Parma, first mentioned by Livy as a fortified vicus near the Padus where a Roman garrison held out during the Gallic uprising of 218 BCE. The Antonine Itinerary and the Tabula Peutingeriana both placed it on this stretch. Archaeologists generally locate it at Taneto, a hamlet of Gattatico near Sant'Ilario d'Enza, though the identification rests on itinerary distances rather than an inscribed find.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Parma
properties.notes: Parma stood on the Via Aemilia as a Roman colonia founded in 183 BCE, the same year as Mutina, and appeared in the Antonine Itinerary as a civitas beyond Tannetum. The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it under the form Parme on the same stretch of the pilgrim road toward Placentia. Modern Parma's cardo and decumanus, still traceable in the city's street grid, run directly along the Roman colonial layout.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Ad Tarum
properties.notes: Ad Tarum, 'at the Tarus,' marked the Via Aemilia's crossing of the river the Romans knew as the Tarus, today's Taro. The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it as a mutatio seven Roman miles out of Parma on the way to Fidentia. The crossing falls near modern Fontanellato or Fontevivo, where the Via Emilia still fords the Taro, though no structure has been excavated at the site.

properties.name: Fidentia
properties.notes: Fidentia appeared in the Antonine Itinerary as 'Fidentiola vicus,' a settlement on the road to Placentia and the site of a battle in 82 BCE where Pompey defeated the Marian general Carrinas. The Itinerarium Burdigalense listed it as a mansio on the same stretch of the pilgrim route. Modern Fidenza grew from the Roman vicus, later renamed Borgo San Donnino in the Middle Ages before reclaiming its ancient name in 1927.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam (Fidentiola vicus)

properties.name: Ad Fonteclos
properties.notes: Ad Fonteclos served as the last mutatio on the Via Aemilia before Placentia, its name pointing to an enclosed spring or fountain along the road. The Itinerarium Burdigalense recorded it on the final stretch out of Fidentia into Placentia. Its site, likely near modern Fiorenzuola d'Arda or Alseno, has not been identified archaeologically.

properties.name: Placentia
properties.notes: Placentia marked the western terminus of the Via Aemilia, standing on the south bank of the Padus where Marcus Aemilius Lepidus completed the road in 187 BCE. The Antonine Itinerary and the Itinerarium Burdigalense both closed their Via Aemilia listings here. Founded as a Latin colony in 218 BCE, Placentia had already withstood a Carthaginian siege by Hannibal before the road connected it directly to Ariminum.
sources: Itin. Ant., Iter ab Arimino Placentiam

properties.name: Genua
properties.notes: Genua served as the western terminus and Tyrrhenian anchor of the Via Postumia, the road consul Spurius Postumius Albinus built in 148 BCE to link Liguria to the Adriatic. The city functioned as Rome's principal Ligurian port, exporting timber, wool, and hides north across the Apennines. A Verona milestone recorded the full Genua-Cremona distance as 122 Roman miles, confirming Genua as the road's official starting point. The road left the city along the Val Polcevera before climbing toward the Apennine passes.
sources: CIL V (Museo Lapidario Maffeiano, Verona milestone, Genua-Cremonam m.p. CXXII)

properties.name: Pons ad Decimum Miliarium
properties.notes: Pons ad Decimum Miliarium marked the point ten Roman miles from Genua where the Via Postumia crossed the Riccio stream on a stone bridge, at the modern Genoa district still called Pontedecimo. The stop sat at the base of the Val Polcevera climb, functioning as the last way-marker before the road began its ascent toward the Apennine crossing near the Bocchetta pass. The name survived unbroken from antiquity into the modern toponym, an unusually direct case of an ancient milestone giving a settlement its permanent name. The original Roman-period bridge was destroyed by flooding in 1834 and replaced nearby.

properties.name: Libarna
properties.notes: Libarna grew into a substantial Roman town on the left bank of the Scrivia river, the only major station the Via Postumia passed between Genua and Dertona. The settlement received a theater, an amphitheater, a forum, and residential quarters, all extensively excavated at the site near modern Serravalle Scrivia. Pliny the Elder, the Antonine Itinerary, and the Tabula Peutingeriana all recorded the town by name. Its position where the road descended from the Apennine crossing made it the last stop before the flat approach to Dertona.

properties.name: Dertona
properties.notes: Dertona, modern Tortona, anchored the western sector of the Via Postumia as the road's first major junction after the Apennine crossing from Genua. The colony connected south to Liguria, west toward Gaul, and east across the Po plain toward Placentia, making it a key node in the Roman road network of Cisalpine Gaul. A Verona milestone recording the total Genua-Cremona distance as 122 Roman miles confirms the 14-mile figure for this leg over a variant manuscript reading of 35 miles. Dertona's status as a colonia gave it walls, a forum, and the administrative apparatus typical of a Roman regional capital.
sources: CIL V (Verona milestone, Genua-Cremonam m.p. CXXII)

properties.name: Iria
properties.notes: Iria stood on the Via Postumia at the crossing of the Staffora river, on the site of modern Voghera. Inscriptions from Aquileia and Dertona recorded its full colonial title as colonia Forum Iulii Iriensium, and the Antonine Itinerary placed it twelve Roman miles north of Dertona. The Roman bridge that carried the road over the Staffora left traces still visible in the modern town. The medieval name Viqueria, which evolved into Voghera, derived directly from the ancient Vicus Iriae.

properties.name: Camillomagus
properties.notes: Camillomagus marked a station on the Via Postumia between Iria and Placentia, generally placed at modern Broni in the Oltrepo Pavese. The Antonine Itinerary and Tabula Peutingeriana recorded it sixteen Roman miles east of Iria and twenty-five miles short of Placentia (already mapped under the Via Aemilia). The site sat along the natural corridor later known as the Stradella strait, a narrow passage between the Apennine foothills and the Po plain that made the location strategically important for controlling east-west traffic. Modern scholarship treats the Broni identification as probable rather than certain, since the ancient settlement itself has not been definitively excavated.

properties.name: Cremona
properties.notes: Cremona anchored the Via Postumia's crossing of the Po river, standing forty-four Roman miles east of Camillomagus by way of Placentia (25 miles Camillomagus-Placentia, then 19 miles Placentia-Cremona; Placentia itself is already mapped as a station under the Via Aemilia and is not duplicated here). Founded as a Latin colony in 218 BCE as a sister settlement to Placentia, Cremona grew into one of the wealthiest cities of Cisalpine Gaul before its sack in 69 CE during the civil wars. A Verona milestone recorded the total distance from Genua to Cremona as 122 Roman miles along this road. East of the city the Via Postumia continued across the plain toward Bedriacum and Verona.
sources: CIL V (Museo Lapidario Maffeiano, Verona milestone, Genua-Cremonam m.p. CXXII)

properties.name: Locus Castorum
properties.notes: Locus Castorum served as a way station roughly midway between Cremona and Bedriacum, taking its name from a roadside shrine to Castor and Pollux that also offered travelers a spring, a rest stop, and a horse-changing point. The location became briefly famous as the site of a battle during the civil war of 69 CE between forces loyal to Otho and Vitellius. Coordinates here are interpolated along the Cremona-Bedriacum road at the 12-mile mark cited in ancient sources, in the area of San Giovanni in Croce and Cappella de' Picenardi, since no modern village has been definitively confirmed as the exact site.

properties.name: Bedriacum
properties.notes: Bedriacum stood at the confluence of the Oglio and Chiese rivers, on the site of modern Calvatone, twenty-two Roman miles east of Cremona along the Via Postumia. The settlement functioned as a major road hub, with routes branching south to Mantua and connecting toward Brescia and the Brenner corridor, in addition to carrying the main Postumia traffic toward Verona. Bedriacum entered the historical record permanently through the two battles fought near it in 69 CE, the Year of the Four Emperors, decisive engagements in the wars between Otho, Vitellius, and Vespasian. Archaeological excavations at Calvatone have uncovered the Roman settlement's street grid and public buildings.

properties.name: Unnamed road junction (Villafranca di Verona)
properties.notes: A road junction on the Via Postumia stood ten Roman miles short of Verona, where the branch road to Mantua split from the main line toward the city; modern Villafranca di Verona occupies this location today. The town's grid of perpendicular streets and its position astride the ancient route suggest Roman-period military or way-station origins beneath the medieval settlement founded in 1185. No ancient Latin name for this junction survives in the itinerary sources, so it is placed here as an unidentified point based on its documented position 10 Roman miles from Verona along the road, rather than as a confirmed named station. Coordinates mark the modern town center as the best available proxy for the ancient junction.

properties.name: Verona
properties.notes: Verona sat at the crossing of the Via Postumia and the Adige river, forty Roman miles east of Bedriacum, and grew into one of the most important cities of Roman Cisalpine Gaul. The Postumia crossed the river here and the city became a major node linking the eastward road toward Vicetia and Aquileia with routes north toward Raetia and the Alps. A milestone preserved today in Verona's Museo Lapidario Maffeiano recorded the full Genua-Cremona distance along this road, underscoring the city's role as a keeper of the road's official record. Verona's amphitheater, forum, and city walls attest to its status as a leading regional colonia.

properties.name: Calidarium
properties.notes: Calidarium marked a stop on the Via Postumia roughly twelve Roman miles east of Verona, at a site known since antiquity for its thermal springs and preserved today in the town name Caldiero. Roman-period bathers used the warm mineral waters for their therapeutic properties, and inscriptions found at the site attest to religious dedications connected to the springs. The location made it a natural resting point for travelers on the road between Verona and Vicetia, combining bathing facilities with lodging. The modern spa at Terme di Giunone continues to draw on the same thermal source the Romans exploited.
sources: Terme di Giunone, site history page

properties.name: Vicetia
properties.notes: Vicetia stood on the Via Postumia thirty-three Roman miles east of Verona, on the site of modern Vicenza, and functioned as a prosperous municipium in the Roman province of Venetia et Histria. The Tabula Peutingeriana and Antonine Itinerary both recorded the thirty-three mile distance from Verona, while the Itinerarium Hierosolymitanum gave a slightly shorter figure of thirty-one miles, a common variance from mile-fraction rounding in the pilgrim source. East of the city the Postumia continued in a long, almost perfectly straight line across the Veneto plain toward the Piave river. A Roman milestone was found nearby at Mason di Montebello, confirming the road's course along this stretch.

properties.name: Flumen Meduacus (Postioma)
properties.notes: Flumen Meduacus marked a mutatio on the Via Postumia thirty-three Roman miles east of Vicetia, at the point the road crossed a branch of the Meduacus river system, on the site of modern Postioma, a hamlet of the comune of Paese near Treviso. The name Postioma itself preserves the road's memory, deriving from the settlement's position where the Via Postumia crossed the older Paleovenetian track along the line of the modern Feltrina road. The stop offered travelers and their horses a change of mounts partway between Vicetia and Opitergium. From here the road continued in a well-documented, nearly straight line toward the Piave crossing and Opitergium.

properties.name: Opitergium
properties.notes: Opitergium stood twenty Roman miles east of the Flumen Meduacus crossing, on the site of modern Oderzo, and served as an important Roman municipium in the Venetian plain. The Via Postumia reached the town after crossing the Piave river on a well-attested, straight alignment, and at the locality still called Tre Piere the road met branch routes running north toward Tridentum and the upper plain. On the Tabula Peutingeriana, Opitergium marks the point where the road's course toward Aquileia becomes less certain in the surviving map. The town's Roman-period street grid and forum area have been documented through excavation beneath the modern city center.

properties.name: Iulia Concordia
properties.notes: Iulia Concordia, founded as a Roman colony in 42 BCE at the site of modern Concordia Sagittaria, marked the point where the Via Postumia met the Via Annia running along the Adriatic coast. The town became a significant production center, especially for weapons manufacture reflected in the epithet Sagittaria ("of the arrows") attached to its modern name. The distance from Opitergium along the Via Postumia proper is not reliably attested: the only figure found, sixteen Roman miles via a secondary route, falls short of the straight-line distance between the two points and is therefore not usable as a confirmed mileage. Concordia's location at the junction of two major roads made it an important administrative and religious center in Roman Venetia.

properties.name: Aquileia
properties.notes: Aquileia served as the eastern terminus of the Via Postumia, standing thirty-one Roman miles from Concordia along the shared final stretch with the Via Annia. Founded as a Latin colony in 181 BCE, Aquileia grew into one of the largest and wealthiest cities of the Roman Empire, a major river port on the Natiso and a gateway for trade and troop movements into Illyricum, Pannonia, and Noricum. The city's forum, port structures, and extensive necropolis have been extensively excavated and form the core of the modern archaeological park. Aquileia's importance as a hub connecting the Cisalpine road network to the Balkan and Danubian provinces made it a fitting eastern anchor for the road system Spurius Postumius Albinus initiated in 148 BCE.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini (Aquileia-Bononia route, Concordia at 31 m.p.)

properties.name: Baccanae (Ad Vacanas)
properties.notes: Baccanae occupied the crater of an extinct volcano twenty-one Roman miles north of Rome on the Via Cassia, at the point where travelers could branch onto the Via Amerina toward Umbria. Archaeologists excavated a large mansio here in 1979 during roadworks, uncovering baths, stables, a portico with a fountain, shops, and barracks built in the first century CE atop Republican-era foundations. The Antonine Itinerary and the Bordeaux Pilgrim both recorded the stop, whose name survived into the Middle Ages as Baccano. The volcanic lake that once filled the crater was drained only in 1838, long after the road had gone out of Roman use.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini (Luca-Roma stage list, Baccanas-Roma XXI)

properties.name: Sutrium
properties.notes: Sutrium commanded the gateway into southern Etruria where the Via Cassia climbed onto the tufa plateau, a position valuable enough that Rome held it as a Latin colony from 383 BCE onward. Its amphitheater, carved directly out of the volcanic rock in the first century CE, still stands beside the ancient road along with an Etruscan-Roman necropolis of rock-cut tombs. The Antonine Itinerary's Luca-Roma stage list places it twelve miles beyond Baccanae and eleven short of Forum Cassii. Modern Sutri preserves the Roman street pattern within its historic core.

properties.name: Vicus Matrini
properties.notes: Vicus Matrini served travelers on the Via Cassia between Sutrium and Forum Cassii, a roadside settlement rather than a full town. Surface surveys near the Casale delle Capannacce, in the comune of Capranica, have recovered early-imperial pottery and building debris consistent with a way-station, though the site has never been formally excavated. The Tabula Peutingeriana lists it seven miles beyond Sutrium and four short of Forum Cassii, exactly matching the Antonine Itinerary's combined eleven-mile figure for that stretch. Its coordinates here are interpolated along the road corridor near Capranica rather than pinned to an excavated structure, since no single geocoded point for the site has been published.

properties.name: Forum Cassii
properties.notes: Forum Cassii grew as a market vicus where the Via Cassia crossed a minor stream about two kilometers northeast of modern Vetralla, forty-four Roman miles from Rome. Four separate ancient itineraries name it: the Antonine Itinerary, the Tabula Peutingeriana, the Ravenna Cosmography, and, centuries later, Archbishop Sigeric's pilgrim route of 990 CE. The medieval church of Santa Maria in Forcassi rose on the site and preserved the Roman name into the present as the frazione Forcassi. Paving slabs of the original road surface still turn up in the surrounding fields.

properties.name: Aquae Passeris
properties.notes: Aquae Passeris was a bathing mansio built around a thermal spring in the Bagnaccio area northeast of Forum Cassii, on the stretch of the Via Cassia approaching Volsinii. The Tabula Peutingeriana records it about twelve miles beyond Forum Cassii, and the sulfurous springs it served still flow today under the name Bagnaccio, just outside modern Viterbo. Travelers used its baths both for hygiene and for the therapeutic reputation Roman spa stations commonly carried on long overland routes. Combined with the following stage to Volsinii, the two legs reproduce the Antonine Itinerary's twenty-eight-mile total for Forum Cassii to Volsinii almost exactly.
sources: Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography (1854), "Via Cassia"

properties.name: Volsinii
properties.notes: Volsinii Novi rose on the northern shore of Lake Bolsena after Rome destroyed the older Etruscan hill-city, traditionally located near modern Orvieto, during a slave revolt in 264 BCE and resettled its population at this lakeside site. The Via Cassia passed directly through the new town, seventy-two Roman miles from Rome according to the Antonine Itinerary's cumulative count, on the long stretch between Forum Cassii and Clusium. Trajan-era Volsinii had temples, baths, and an amphitheater whose remains still stand beside modern Bolsena, and its cults and elite families are well attested in inscriptions. Its most famous relic, the miracle of the bleeding host at the church of Santa Cristina, belongs to a much later, medieval layer of the site's history.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini (Via Cassia, cumulative LXXII m.p. ab Urbe)

properties.name: Clusium
properties.notes: Clusium ranked among the twelve cities of the Etruscan league and, under its king Lars Porsenna, briefly held Rome itself at the end of the sixth century BCE. The Via Cassia reached it around the hundredth Roman mile from Rome, after descending from Volsinii through the upper Val di Chiana. Its painted tomb chambers and museum of Etruscan and Roman antiquities make it one of the best-documented stops on the entire road. From Clusium the Via Cassia continued north to Arretium, a stretch the Antonine Itinerary breaks only at the otherwise-unidentified station of Ad Statuas.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini (Via Cassia, cumulative ~CII m.p. ab Urbe)

properties.name: Ad Statuas
properties.notes: Ad Statuas appears in the Antonine Itinerary as a stage twelve Roman miles north of Clusium and twenty-five short of Arretium, its name suggesting a roadside marker or shrine hung with statues rather than a real town. No inscription or excavated structure has ever been tied to the name, and proposals have ranged across the Val di Chiana between Chiusi and Cortona without agreement. The point plotted here is a proportional placement along the Clusium-Arretium road corridor, chosen to satisfy the itinerary's own mileage figures rather than any excavated findspot. Confidence in the exact location is accordingly low.
sources: Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography (1854), "Via Cassia"

properties.name: Arretium
properties.notes: Arretium was one of Etruria's foremost cities long before the Via Cassia reached it, famous by the early Empire for the glossy red "Arretine ware" pottery its workshops exported across the Mediterranean. The Antonine Itinerary places it on the Cassia's northern stretch, and travelers in 117 CE could pick up connecting roads east toward Umbria and the Via Flaminia network. Substantial Roman remains survive beneath modern Arezzo, including a well-preserved amphitheater and fragments of the forum. From here the Via Cassia turned north again for the run down the Arno valley to Florentia.

properties.name: Ad Fines (Casas Caesarianas)
properties.notes: The Antonine Itinerary records this stage under two alternative names, Ad Fines and Casas Caesarianas, twenty-five Roman miles north of Arretium on the road down to Florentia, but gives no further description. Neither name has been matched to a confirmed site, and the stretch runs through the upper Arno valley near modern Montevarchi and Figline Valdarno, an area of continuous medieval and modern settlement that has likely obscured any Roman remains. The point plotted here is a proportional placement along the Arretium-Florentia corridor rather than an excavated findspot. Its dual naming may reflect an imperial estate ("Caesarian houses") that absorbed an older boundary station on this stretch of the road.

properties.name: Florentia
properties.notes: Florentia began as a Roman colony on the Arno in the first century BCE, planted below the older Etruscan hill-town of Faesulae, and by Trajan's reign had grown into the northern terminus the Via Cassia had been built to reach. From here roads continued on to Pistoria and Luca, linking the Cassia into the wider network of northern Italy. The colony's original street grid still underlies Florence's historic center, and fragments of its amphitheater and baths survive within later buildings. A Hadrianic milestone of 124 CE records repairs to the Via Cassia along the eighty-six-mile stretch between the territory of Clusium and Florentia.

properties.name: Careiae
properties.notes: Careiae was the first station the Via Clodia reached after it split from the Via Cassia near modern La Storta, an Etruscan-founded town whose Roman-period life is attested by inscriptions including a statue base dedicated by the local guild of dendrophori. Its ruins lie in the abandoned settlement of Galeria, about a kilometer west of the modern hamlet of Santa Maria di Galeria, on a low ridge above the Arrone stream. Surface remains of the Clodia's paving survive nearby within the site's grounds. The distance given here follows modern scholarship's roughly 25-kilometer estimate of Careiae's position from Rome rather than a directly reconciled itinerary figure.

properties.name: Ad Novas
properties.notes: Ad Novas was a horse-changing mutatio on the Via Clodia's approach to Lake Sabatinus, sited near modern Vigna di Valle on the lake's southern shore. The Tabula Peutingeriana records it nine miles short of Forum Clodii, a figure that closely matches the measured distance between the area's thermal springs and the hill of San Liberato, where Forum Clodii stood. No structural remains have been formally excavated at the site, and its exact position is inferred from itinerary distances rather than direct archaeological confirmation.

properties.name: Forum Clodii
properties.notes: Forum Clodii stood on the hill of San Liberato above the western shore of Lake Bracciano, a market town the Antonine Itinerary places thirty-two Roman miles from Rome on the Via Clodia. Excavations have exposed baths, a forum, and a temple complex, and the site takes its name from the road's presumed builder or patron, a member of the Claudian family. The eighth- or ninth-century church of Saints Marcus, Marcianus, and Liberatus was later built over the Roman remains, preserving the site's identity into the modern toponym San Liberato. Forum Clodii issued its own coinage under Augustus, evidence of a self-governing community rather than a mere waypoint.

properties.name: Blera
properties.notes: Blera perched on a narrow tufa spur between two ravines, a defensive Etruscan site whose peak came in the sixth and fifth centuries BCE, long before the Via Clodia formalized the road running past it. The Roman-era bridges known today as the Ponte della Rocca and Ponte del Diavolo carried the ancient road across the ravines flanking the town and still stand. The Tabula Peutingeriana places it twenty-two miles beyond Forum Clodii, deep in the hill country of the Tuscia. Modern Blera retains its Roman-derived name and sits directly on the identified line of the ancient road.

properties.name: Marta (Norchia)
properties.notes: The Tabula Peutingeriana records a station called Marta nine miles beyond Blera, but that distance falls well short of the Marta river and modern town further north, leading topographers to place the ancient stage instead at Norchia, an Etruscan settlement famous for its cliffside rock-cut tomb facades. The Via Clodia crossed the Biedano river gorge nearby through the Cava Buia, a roughly 400-meter road-cutting with walls up to ten meters high, one of the most dramatic surviving stretches of the road. Norchia's necropolis, carved with temple-front tomb facades in the Hellenistic period, remained in use into the Roman era even as the settlement itself declined. The identification of this stage with the itinerary's "Marta" is a scholarly proposal based on mileage fit rather than an inscribed certainty.

properties.name: Tuscania
properties.notes: Tuscania was a substantial Etruscan and Roman town on the Via Clodia, walled and equipped with temples whose terracotta revetments rank among the finest Etrusco-Italic architectural sculpture ever recovered. The Tabula Peutingeriana names it as a stage on the Clodia's run toward the Maremma coast, though the precise ancient mileage from the previous station has not survived and is estimated here from the road's known course rather than a cited figure. Two large Etruscan necropoleis flank the town, including the Curunas family's painted sarcophagi now in the local archaeological museum. Medieval Tuscania absorbed much of the Roman town's fabric, and its two Romanesque basilicas stand on early Christian foundations at the ancient site's edge.

properties.name: Maternum
properties.notes: Maternum appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana as a stage on the Via Clodia between Tuscania and Saturnia, roughly eighteen kilometers past the former and twenty-seven short of the latter, but no inscription or excavated site carries the name. Nineteenth-century topographers split between Canino and Ischia di Castro as the likely modern equivalent, both hill towns in the lower Fiora valley that controlled the same stretch of road, and the question remains unresolved. The coordinates plotted here follow the Ischia di Castro identification, the placement that best satisfies the itinerary's combined mileage to Saturnia; the alternative Canino site lies roughly the same distance away but fails a straight-line consistency check against the sourced distance to Saturnia. Confidence in this identification is low, and the point should be read as an approximate stage rather than a fixed archaeological findspot.
sources: Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography (1854), "Via Clodia"

properties.name: Saturnia
properties.notes: Saturnia became a Roman colony in 183 BCE, its walls rebuilt in massive polygonal blocks that still ring the hilltop today, and the road's later medieval name, "the road of the springs," refers to the sulfurous thermal waters that rise nearby. The colony marked the practical endpoint of the well-attested stretch of the Via Clodia; beyond it, the road's course toward a junction with the Via Aurelia near Cosa is inferred rather than traced on the ground. Saturnia's forum, streets, and necropolis have been partly excavated within and around the medieval walled village that now occupies the site. Its free-flowing hot springs, the Cascate del Mulino, remain a popular bathing spot fed by the same waters Roman visitors used two millennia ago.

properties.name: Lorium
properties.notes: Lorium was the first posting station out of Rome on the Via Aurelia, twelve Roman miles along the coast road. Antoninus Pius later kept a country villa here and died in it in 161, a mark of how fashionable this stretch became in the following century.

properties.name: Ad Turres
properties.notes: A minor horse-change stop on the coast road between Lorium and Pyrgi, named for a line of watchtowers along this stretch. No structure has been excavated and identified with certainty, so its position is placed along the known road corridor rather than pinned to a specific ruin.

properties.name: Pyrgi
properties.notes: Pyrgi was the harbor of the Etruscan city of Caere, home to a sanctuary of Uni-Astarte where three gold tablets with Etruscan and Phoenician inscriptions were unearthed in 1964. A medieval castle now stands over the ancient port at Santa Severa.

properties.name: Castrum Novum
properties.notes: Rome founded this coastal colony in 264 BCE alongside Pyrgi to guard Caere's shoreline during the First Punic War. Excavations at Torre Chiaruccia near Santa Marinella have uncovered its theater, curia, and public aqueduct.

properties.name: Centumcellae
properties.notes: Trajan built this artificial harbor to relieve pressure on Ostia, finishing it around 106-107. It grew into the chief town of the northern Etrurian coast, and its modern name Civitavecchia still means "old city."

properties.name: Graviscae
properties.notes: Graviscae served as the port of Etruscan Tarquinii before Rome refounded it as a colony in 181 BCE at the mouth of the Marta river. A sanctuary here to Aphrodite-Turan drew dedications from Greek, Etruscan, and Phoenician traders alike.

properties.name: Forum Aurelii
properties.notes: A market town that grew up on the Via Aurelia itself, distinct from the older Etruscan city of Vulci nearby. Travelers used it as a resupply stop on the long coastal stretch toward Cosa.

properties.name: Cosa
properties.notes: Rome planted this hilltop colony above the Tyrrhenian coast in 273 BCE. Its polygonal walls, forum, and capitolium still stand largely intact, alongside an artificial harbor built at the base of the hill.

properties.name: Telamon
properties.notes: Telamon's harbor sits at the foot of Monte Argentario, where a Roman army crushed a Gallic-Samnite coalition in 225 BCE. The itinerary sources for this exact stretch of coast are too damaged to fix a reliable mileage from Cosa, so no distance figure is given.

properties.name: Populonium
properties.notes: Populonia is the only major Etruscan and Roman city built directly on the Tyrrhenian shore, and it smelted iron ore shipped over from Elba. Its acropolis and the Baratti necropolis below have been extensively excavated. As with Telamon, the surviving itinerary mileage for this stretch is too corrupt to give a reliable figure.

properties.name: Vada Volaterrana
properties.notes: This was the port and saltworks of inland Volaterrae, with a large warehouse complex and a coastal sanctuary that stayed in use for centuries. Roman milestones found nearby confirm the coast road's course through the district.

properties.name: Ad Herculem
properties.notes: A small way-station on the final leg into Pisae, named for a roadside shrine to Hercules. No ruin has been securely tied to the name, so it is placed along the known road corridor between Vada and Pisae.

properties.name: Pisae
properties.notes: Pisae sat where the Arno and Auser rivers met the sea, an Etruscan port that became a Roman colony and naval base in 180 BCE. The Via Aurelia effectively ended here before continuing north as the Via Aemilia Scauri toward Luna and Genua.

properties.name: Taberna Frigida
properties.notes: This station marked the crossing of the Frigidus river on the coast road north of Pisae. The medieval church of San Leonardo al Frigido, built on the site, still preserves the ancient name.

properties.name: Luna
properties.notes: Luna was a Roman colony founded in 177 BCE at the mouth of the Magra river, built rich on the marble its quarries sent to Rome — the same quarries now called Carrara. Its amphitheater and forum survive, and the site is already on this map as the curated city of Luni.

properties.name: Fidenae
properties.notes: Fidenae stood on a plateau above the Tiber only eight kilometers from Rome, close enough that the two cities fought repeated wars over it in the earliest days of the Republic. Rock-cut tombs from the same period still line the cliffs north of the site.

properties.name: Eretum
properties.notes: Eretum sat where the Via Salaria met the Via Nomentana, on a Sabine hilltop identified with modern Casacotta. The nearby Colle del Forno necropolis shows the site was lived in continuously from the Iron Age straight through the Roman period.

properties.name: Vicus Novus
properties.notes: This road station stood at the traditional 33rd milestone of the Via Salaria, near modern Osteria Nuova. A large Roman tomb chamber known locally as "Li Massacci" still marks the crossroads.

properties.name: Reate
properties.notes: Reate was the chief town of the Sabine hill country, where the Via Salaria crossed the Velino river valley. The Flavian family kept property in the district, a connection that ran deep into local memory by 117.

properties.name: Cutiliae
properties.notes: A sulfur-spring spa east of Reate on the shore of the Lacus Cutiliensis, developed as a bathing resort under the early emperors. This is the same site as this map's Aquae Cutiliae health-axis entry, listed again here as its own stage on the Via Salaria's road network.

properties.name: Interocrium
properties.notes: Interocrium sat in the narrow Velino gorge at modern Antrodoco, where the Via Salaria began its climb into the central Apennines. The name itself, "among the peaks," describes the site's position at a junction of two mountain passes.

properties.name: Forum Decii
properties.notes: A market village on the road between Interocrium and Falacrinae, recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana as "Foroecri." Its exact site in the upper Velino valley near modern Bacugno has never been excavated.

properties.name: Falacrinae
properties.notes: Falacrinae was a small village in the Sabine highlands and the birthplace of the emperor Vespasian in 9 CE, as Suetonius records. A large first-century villa complex excavated near Cittareale in 2009 is identified with the site.

properties.name: Ad Martis
properties.notes: A mansio named for a roadside altar to Mars, recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana between Falacrinae and the Apennine crossing. It is identified with the modern hamlet of Tufo, a frazione of Arquata del Tronto.

properties.name: Vicus Badies
properties.notes: A station recorded on the road between Falacrinae and the Apennine pass into Picenum, linked in local tradition to the Fonte del Campo area near Accumoli. No structural remains have been securely tied to the name.

properties.name: Ad Centesimum
properties.notes: Named for standing roughly at the hundredth Roman mile from the city, this station covered the upper Tronto valley stretch of the Via Salaria. A Roman bridge nearby at Quintodecimo still marks the crossing, and the district's hot springs later gave the modern town its name, Acquasanta Terme.

properties.name: Asculum Picenum
properties.notes: Asculum was the chief city of the Picentes before Rome absorbed the region, and the spark of the Social War of 91 BCE began here with the massacre of Rome's officials. A Roman bridge, the Ponte di Solestà, still carries traffic across the Tronto today.

properties.name: Castrum Truentinum
properties.notes: This fortified port at the mouth of the Truentus river was the Adriatic terminus of the Via Salaria, where salt first came ashore for the long haul inland to Rome. The site is identified with modern Martinsicuro on the river's right bank.

properties.name: Forum Novum
properties.notes: Excavations at Piano Sant'Arcangelo near Paduli uncovered a stone-paved stretch of the Via Traiana with cart-wheel ruts still visible in the surface, along with roadside structures belonging to this vicus. It served as the first stopping point out of Beneventum, about 10 Roman miles down the road, and forms part of the Via Appia UNESCO World Heritage listing inscribed in 2024.
sources: Soprintendenza ABAP Caserta e Benevento — excavation report at Forum Novum, Paduli
Appia Day — Appia Traiana: Forum Novum al Miglio X, appiaday.org

properties.name: Aequum Tuticum
properties.notes: Aequum Tuticum grew up on a plateau above the Miscano valley where the Via Traiana crossed the Via Herculia, near modern Ariano Irpino. Surveys of the site, known locally as San Eleuterio, have mapped its forum and public buildings; the Antonine Itinerary places it 21 Roman miles from Beneventum.

properties.name: Aecae
properties.notes: Aecae sat on a hilltop east of the Apennine watershed and gave its name directly to the medieval and modern town of Troia built on the same site. It was the first major stop the Via Traiana reached after descending from the mountains into Apulia.

properties.name: Herdonia
properties.notes: Herdonia was sacked during the Second Punic War and later rebuilt as a Roman municipium on the Tavoliere plain. Decades of excavation there uncovered its forum, an amphitheater, and bath buildings spanning the Republican through late antique periods.

properties.name: Canusium
properties.notes: Canusium was a major wool- and textile-trading city on the Ofanto river, and the Via Traiana crossed the river there on a Roman bridge whose remains still stand. Trajan raised a monumental arch at Canusium to mark the road, part of which survives today.
sources: Fondazione Archeologica Canosina — Percorrendo la Via Traiana, canusium.it

properties.name: Rudas
properties.notes: The Tabula Peutingeriana places Rudas as a waypoint on the Via Traiana between Canusium and Rubi, in territory later belonging to Andria. No structures have been firmly matched to the name, though researchers have proposed a location near Masseria Santa Tavella south of the road's traced course.

properties.name: Rubi
properties.notes: Rubi was a Peucetian town that minted its own coinage before Roman rule and later became known for the red-figure pottery recovered from its tombs. Horace called his travel party weary on reaching Rubi in 37 BCE and complained the road there had turned worse from rain, decades before Trajan paved this stretch as the Via Traiana.

properties.name: Butuntum
properties.notes: Butuntum grew into a Roman municipium on the Via Traiana between Rubi and Barium, set amid the olive-growing territory that still defines Bitonto today. The Antonine Itinerary lists it as a single day's stage short of the Adriatic coast at Barium.

properties.name: Barium
properties.notes: Horace called Bari's walls piscosi... moenia Bari (fish-rich Bari) when he passed through on this same coastal corridor in 37 BCE, decades before Trajan paved it as the Via Traiana in 109 CE. The new road gave the Adriatic fishing port a direct paved route back to Beneventum and on to Rome.

properties.name: Turris Iuliana
properties.notes: Turris Iuliana appears in the fourth-century Itinerarium Burdigalense as a horse-changing stop on the coast road south of Barium, in the area later called Scamuso near Torre a Mare. No Roman remains at the site have been separated out from the later coastal towers built over the same ground.
sources: Bari Torre a Mare local history note

properties.name: Turres Aureliae
properties.notes: The Antonine Itinerary places Turres Aureliae 21 Roman miles south of Barium, on the stretch of coast where Torre Cintola near Monopoli now stands. Excavations at Torre Cintola have documented a multi-period coastal settlement that continued to serve as a landing point on this road into the medieval era.
sources: Il contesto pluristratificato di Torre Cintola a Monopoli (BA)

properties.name: Egnatia
properties.notes: Egnatia was a Messapian port town absorbed into Roman Apulia, and its ruins at the Savelletri archaeological park still show a forum, basilica, and an early Christian church. Horace mocked the town in the same 37 BCE satire, ridiculing a local priestly claim that incense caught fire on its altar without any flame.

properties.name: Ad Decimum
properties.notes: The mutatio Ad Decimum took its name from its position at the tenth Roman mile along this stretch, now identified with Torre San Leonardo on the Apulian coast between Egnazia and Speluncae. As a mutatio it existed to change horses for the cursus publicus rather than to lodge travelers overnight.
sources: FederArcheo — Ostuni (Br). Mutatio ad Decimum, Torre San Leonardo, Masseria Pilone

properties.name: Speluncae
properties.notes: The mansio Ad Speluncas has been identified with Torre Santa Sabina in the comune of Carovigno, where Roman-era structures were found in the Mezzaluna locality near the shore. It was the last overnight stop before travelers reached Brundisium, 19 Roman miles further down the coast.
sources: Brindisiweb.it — La viabilita e le opere stradali in epoca romana

properties.name: Ad Sextum
properties.notes: The first change of horses out of Singidunum, six Roman miles down the road and named for the milestone that marked it. The Bordeaux pilgrim swapped teams here in 333 CE before the run east along the Danube bluffs. Belgrade's Mali Mokri Lug grew over the spot, and the Ottoman road to Constantinople later reused the same line.

properties.name: Tricornium
properties.notes: A Danube fort and horse-change twelve miles out from Singidunum, garrisoned to hold the Upper Moesian frontier. Nineteenth-century antiquaries recorded the walls of Castra Tricornia on the river terrace at Ritopek. A soldier's bronze breastplate engraved with seven planetary deities came out of the site.

properties.name: Ad Sextum Miliarem
properties.notes: A change of horses seven miles on from Tricornium, named like its neighbour for a roadside milestone. The road ran here on the terrace above the Danube, carrying dispatches between the legionary bases at Singidunum and Viminacium. Modern Grocka covers the station.

properties.name: Mons Aureus
properties.notes: The Golden Mountain held the Danube bank six miles east of Grocka with an auxiliary fort and a civil settlement attached. The Bordeaux Itinerary ranked it a town rather than a mere relay. Its remains lie under the village of Seone in the Smederevo district.

properties.name: Vinceia
properties.notes: A change of horses six miles from Mons Aureus, counted among the principal towns of Moesia Superior. It stood where the Morava traffic came down to meet the Danube trunk road. Smederevo's great fortress later rose on the same strategic ground.

properties.name: Margum
properties.notes: Nine miles past Vinceia the road reached Margum, the fortified town at the mouth of the Great Morava. Travellers crossed the river here before the last ten miles into Viminacium. The site lies at Dubravica outside Pozarevac, where the Roman town was refortified again under the Byzantines.

properties.name: Ad Octavum
properties.notes: A change of horses set nine miles short of Horreum Margi, its name counting the eighth milestone from the halt behind it. The Bordeaux pilgrim passed through in 333 CE coming down the Resava valley. Here the road left the hill country of the Kucaj for the open Morava plain.

properties.name: Horreum Margi
properties.notes: The granary of the Morava, where the trunk road crossed the river. Rome founded it as a fort, gave it a shield factory, and raised it to municipium before 224 CE. The Bordeaux pilgrim broke his journey here for the night; the excavated remains now sit inside Cuprija.

properties.name: Sarmatorum
properties.notes: A change of horses twelve miles south of Horreum Margi, named for the Sarmatians settled along this reach of the Morava. The Bordeaux Itinerary marked the boundary between Moesia and Dacia at this point in the road. Teams were swapped here before the eleven-mile pull to Cametas.

properties.name: Cametas
properties.notes: Eleven miles on from the Sarmatian post, a change of horses on the road up the Morava corridor. The Bordeaux pilgrim counted nine more miles from here to his overnight halt at Praesidium Pompei. The station stood where the town of Razanj now sits.

properties.name: Praesidium Pompei
properties.notes: An overnight halt nine miles beyond Cametas, run as a garrisoned post on the Morava road. The Antonine Itinerary placed it thirty-three miles short of Naissus. Its remains lie at Bovan near Aleksinac, in the gorge where the Moravica breaks through the hills.

properties.name: Rappiana
properties.notes: The last change of horses before Naissus, twelve miles out from Praesidium Pompei and twelve miles short of the city. The Bordeaux pilgrim logged it in 333 CE on the road up the South Morava. Archaeologists working the Aleksinac district have narrowed the site to a handful of candidates.

properties.name: Redicibus
properties.notes: Twelve miles east of Naissus the road entered the Sicevo gorge, and a change of horses waited at Redicibus. The Bordeaux pilgrim named it in 333 CE between the city and the halt at Remesiana. The Nisava cut the only practical way through these mountains, and the road clung to its bank.

properties.name: Remesiana
properties.notes: An overnight halt sixteen miles beyond Redicibus that grew into a walled town and a bishopric. Niceta of Remesiana preached and wrote here in the fourth century. Bela Palanka covers the site, where a milestone of Severus Alexander has come to light.

properties.name: Latina
properties.notes: A change of horses nine miles east of Remesiana, its name marking the stretch where Latin speech dominated the road. The Bordeaux pilgrim stopped here before the nine-mile run on to Turres. The station sits at Crnokliste in the Pirot district.

properties.name: Turres
properties.notes: The Towers stood nine miles on from Latina and served as the main halt between Naissus and Serdica. This was no bare stable but a market town where the traffic of two cities met, with legionaries stationed to keep the road open. Its foundations, nearly four metres wide, survive under Pirot Fortress.

properties.name: Meldia
properties.notes: An overnight halt thirty-one miles east of Turres, the last mansio before the descent into Serdica. The Bordeaux pilgrim reached it after two changes of horses at Translitis and Ballanstra. It lay in the corridor between Dragoman and Slivnitsa, where the road leaves the pass for the Sofia basin.

properties.name: Scretisca
properties.notes: The first stop west of Serdica, twelve miles out, and far more than a stable. Constantine the Great kept a residence here, and both the palatium and the road station were excavated at Kostinbrod from 1973. The Bordeaux pilgrim changed horses here eleven miles short of the city gates.

properties.name: Extuomne
properties.notes: Eight miles east of Serdica the road reached its first change of horses, logged by the Bordeaux pilgrim in 333 CE. The stop served traffic bound for the Vakarel watershed and the Thracian plain beyond. It stood on the flat ground east of the city where the road ran clear of the Iskar.

properties.name: Buragara
properties.notes: An overnight halt nine miles past Extuomne, substantial enough to count as a full road station. Bulgarian archaeologists excavated a road watchtower and its small attached settlement by Lesnovo, southwest of Elin Pelin. Travellers rested here before the climb toward the Sredna Gora.

properties.name: Bona Mansio
properties.notes: One of the very few stations on this road that archaeologists have actually found and dug. Excavation from 2016 exposed a stone-and-brick circuit wall 2.60 metres thick, standing over three metres high, with its main gate intact. The complex ran from the fourth century to the late sixth, when raiders burned it out. It sits beside Karabunar in the Septemvri district.

properties.name: Bessapara
properties.notes: The Market of the Bessi, an overnight halt twenty-one miles beyond Bona Mansio on the Hebros plain. Rome kept the Thracian tribal name after breaking the Bessi and fixed it to the station. The record knows an Upper and a Lower Bessapara; the site lies by Sinitovo near Pazardzhik.

properties.name: Cillae
properties.notes: An overnight halt nine miles west of Carassura on the run from Philippopolis toward the Hebros crossings. The Bordeaux pilgrim reached it after two changes of horses out of the city, at Sernota and Paramuole. The road here ran dead straight across the open Thracian plain.

properties.name: Carassura
properties.notes: A change of horses nine miles east of Cillae that grew into a fortified late-antique settlement. A joint Bulgarian-German team excavated the station and its fortress at Rupkite near Chirpan. The name outlived Rome: a medieval village reoccupied the ruins and kept it.

properties.name: Nicae
properties.notes: An overnight halt east of Hadrianopolis, founded as Nike and carrying the name down to Ottoman Havsa. The battle that destroyed Valens and two-thirds of his field army in 378 CE was fought beside this station. The Bordeaux pilgrim slept here on his way to Constantinople.

properties.name: Urisio
properties.notes: A change of horses seven miles west of Bergule, logged by the Bordeaux pilgrim in 333 CE. It served the stretch running out of the Hebros country into the plain of eastern Thrace. The settlement was still inhabited in Byzantine times.

properties.name: Bergule
properties.notes: An overnight halt seven miles east of Urisio that grew into a town and was renamed Arcadiopolis. It sat on a tributary of the Ergene, roughly halfway between Hadrianopolis and Constantinople, and became a bishopric. Luleburgaz covers the site.

properties.name: Narco
properties.notes: A change of horses eight miles east of Bergule on the flat Thracian road. The Bordeaux pilgrim used it in 333 CE between Bergule and the halt at Drizipara. The settlement survived into Byzantine times.

properties.name: Drizipara
properties.notes: An overnight halt nine miles past Narco that became a bishopric of the province of Europa. The Antonine Itinerary set it fourteen miles from Bergule on the run to Byzantium. Buyukkaristiran, in the Luleburgaz district, stands on the site.

properties.name: Tipso
properties.notes: A change of horses eight miles beyond Drizipara, on the open ground northwest of Tzurulum. The Bordeaux pilgrim named it in 333 CE. The station served the long flat crossing of the Ergene basin.

properties.name: Tzurulum
properties.notes: The overnight halt the Bordeaux pilgrim reached on his fifth night out of Hadrianopolis. The hill town commanded the point where the road turned south for the Propontis, and Byzantine armies refortified it again and again. Corlu grew on the same ridge.

properties.name: Beodizo
properties.notes: The last change of horses before Heraclea, set nine miles northwest of the old Perinthus. The Bordeaux pilgrim logged it in 333 CE. The site lies by Turkgucu outside Corlu, where the road came down off the ridge toward the Marmara shore.

properties.name: Baunne
properties.notes: A change of horses twelve miles east of Heraclea on the coastal run to Constantinople. The Bordeaux pilgrim used it in 333 CE, ten miles short of Selymbria. The road here followed the Marmara shore within sight of the water.

properties.name: Callum
properties.notes: A change of horses ten miles east of Selymbria, the second-to-last relay before the capital. The Bordeaux pilgrim named it in 333 CE. A seventeenth-century traveller was still able to point out its ruins on the coast road.

properties.name: Altinum
properties.notes: The eastern trailhead on the Adriatic lagoon, a wealthy trading port before Rome ever laid a road north. Two branches of the Via Claudia Augusta left the Po valley for the Alps -- this the eastern one, the other starting upriver at Hostilia -- and met again at Tridentum.

properties.name: Hostilia
properties.notes: The western trailhead on the Po, where boats from Ravenna and Mantua unloaded onto the new Alpine road. Drusus broke ground here in 15 BCE; his stepson Claudius finished the job and put his own name on it in 46-47 CE.

properties.name: Mansio Servasa
properties.notes: A rest stop dug out of the Adige gorge near Brentino, north of Verona, on the likely line of the road north to Tridentum. Excavators found a forge with its furnace still in place, guest rooms, and a marble threshold worn by centuries of travelers' feet.

properties.name: Trento
properties.notes: Both Alpine branches of the road met here, at the point where the Adige valley narrows and turns for the mountains. A Roman municipium since Claudius's day, its street grid still underlies the modern city center.

properties.name: Pons Drusi
properties.notes: A bridge over the Isarco/Talvera, named for Drusus, that grew into the town of Bolzano. In 117 CE it was still a road-post at a river crossing, not yet the market town it would become.

properties.name: Endidae
properties.notes: A staging post on the Adige at Egna, its foundations rediscovered and restored in recent years. The Antonine Itinerary places it 23 Roman miles north of Tridentum -- exactly the modern road distance to Egna, a rare case where the ancient figure and the ground still agree.

properties.name: Maia
properties.notes: The statio at Merano, where the road left the Adige for the Passer valley on its climb toward the Reschen Pass. The name survives almost unchanged in the district of Maia Bassa/Untermais.

properties.name: Rabland milestone
properties.notes: One of only two Via Claudia Augusta milestones ever found still in something like its original setting, pulled from the Vinschgau roadbed near Naturno. Its inscription is among the oldest Roman writing recovered anywhere in the Alps.

properties.name: Inutrium
properties.notes: A post at Nauders, right at the Reschen Pass summit -- at 1,507m the highest point the road reaches. It is the only station on this whole Alpine crossing that a surviving ancient source names outright rather than leaving to archaeology.

properties.name: Foetibus
properties.notes: A stop on the Lech at Fussen, where the road came down off the mountains into the province of Raetia proper before the last stretch to Augusta Vindelicum.

properties.name: Augusta Vindelicum
properties.notes: Augsburg today, and the road's real destination -- the provincial capital of Raetia that Drusus and Claudius spent sixty years of road-building trying to connect to the Adriatic. Not yet on this map as a full city; the road stops here for now.

properties.name: Submuntorium
properties.notes: A fort and river-post on the upper Danube where a spur of the road reached the frontier, roughly 30km north of Augsburg. Some scholars place the name at nearby Neuburg instead of Burghofe -- the site is secure, the exact ancient label less so.

properties.name: Ponte Mammolo
properties.notes: A bridge over the Aniene just outside Rome's walls, the first landmark on the road out to Tibur. The modern bridge on the same site still carries the road's descendant highway.

properties.name: Aquae Albulae
properties.notes: A statio at the sulfur springs six kilometers short of Tibur, their milky-blue water so strong-smelling that Pliny, Strabo and Isidore all singled it out. Romans travelled out from the city just to bathe here, the way people still do today at the same springs.

properties.name: Vicovaro
properties.notes: Vicus Varia sat where the road left the Aniene valley for the climb toward the Aequian hills, at the point the Via Sublacensis split off toward Subiaco. Its name survives almost unchanged in the modern town.

properties.name: Carseoli
properties.notes: A Latin colony planted in Aequian territory in 298 BCE, well before the road that would later run through it. By 117 CE it was a working stop on the climb toward the Fucine Lake basin.

properties.name: Alba Fucens
properties.notes: A frontier colony planted in 303 BCE between the Marsi and the Aequi, high on the shoulder of Monte Velino above the Fucine Lake. Rome kept its most dangerous prisoners here -- Syphax of Numidia died in custody at Alba Fucens, and King Perseus of Macedon, the last man to rule as a Hellenistic king, ended his life here too.

properties.name: Marruvium
properties.notes: The chief town of the Marsi, on the eastern shore of the Fucine Lake -- a people Rome fought hard against in the Social War and then leaned on hard for legionaries afterward. The lake itself, since drained, made the town a lakeside stop rather than the landlocked ruin it is today.

properties.name: Corfinio
properties.notes: The Italian rebels of the Social War made Corfinium their capital in 91 BCE and renamed it Italica -- a rival Rome built to hold its own name and its own senate. It lost that war and went back to being an ordinary Roman town, but the memory of the challenge stuck to the place for a long time after.

properties.name: Interpromium
properties.notes: A relay station in the Aternus valley below modern San Valentino in Abruzzo Citeriore. The Itineraries give it as 12 Roman miles from Corfinium, but that figure doesn't square with the geodesic distance between the two identified sites closely enough to trust on this ground-coordinate precision, so it ships unclaimed here rather than forced.

properties.name: Chieti
properties.notes: Teate, chief town of the Marrucini, sat on a hill above the Aternus valley -- a defensible perch that is why modern Chieti still looks down on the Pescara plain from the same spot.

properties.name: Pescara
properties.notes: The road's Adriatic terminus, where the Aternus river reaches the sea -- 9 Roman miles past Teate by the Itineraries' own count, and 21 from Interpromium, both figures the ground still bears out. A modest port town in 117 CE, nothing like the city that grew from it.

properties.name: Nola
properties.notes: The first major stop south of Capua on the road to Rhegium, and later the town where Augustus died on 19 August 14 CE. A specific Antonine Itinerary mileage for this leg turned up in only one unreliable source, so no distance figure is claimed here.
sources: Itinerarium Antonini, Regium-Capuam route (loose citation, exact section unconfirmed)

properties.name: Nuceria Alfaterna
properties.notes: Modern Nocera Superiore/Inferiore. The Republican-era Lapis Pollae milestone (CIL I2 638), found at Forum Popilii, gives 51 Roman miles from there to Nuceria — the strongest single piece of evidence placing this town squarely on the Via Popilia mainline.

properties.name: Salernum
properties.notes: Modern Salerno. A Latin colony planted in 194 BCE on the Gulf of Salerno, partly to hold the coast after the Picentini were resettled inland — it sat directly on the road south toward the Vallo di Diano.

properties.name: Picentia
properties.notes: Modern Pontecagnano Faiano. Resettled with Picentes displaced from the Adriatic coast in 268 BCE; whether it sat on the Via Popilia's mainline or a coastal spur is not fully settled in the sources found.
sources: Princeton Encyclopedia of Classical Sites, s.v. Picentia (via search)

properties.name: Eburum
properties.notes: Modern Eboli, the gateway from the Sele coastal plain into the Vallo di Diano interior that the road follows south.

properties.name: Acerronia
properties.notes: Near modern Auletta, a waystation on the Vallo di Diano stretch of the road between Eburum and the Nares Lucanae narrows.

properties.name: Nares Lucanae
properties.notes: "The Narrows of Lucania," a mountain passage near Sicignano degli Alburni whose exact location is disputed between three nearby candidate sites — shipped here as the interpolated corridor midpoint rather than a specific excavated spot.

properties.name: Atina
properties.notes: Modern Atena Lucana, one of a tight cluster of stations serving the Vallo di Diano valley floor.

properties.name: Consilinum
properties.notes: Modern Sala Consilina preserves the Roman name almost unchanged, one of the more securely identified stops in the Vallo di Diano.

properties.name: Marcellianum
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at San Giovanni in Fonte, later home to a paleochristian baptistery Cassiodorus is recorded visiting in the early 6th century.
sources: Comune di Sala Consilina, local history pages (via search)

properties.name: Tegianum
properties.notes: Modern Teggiano, another Vallo di Diano stop on the road south toward the Lucanian mountains.

properties.name: Forum Popilii
properties.notes: Modern Polla — the town literally named for the consul who built this road, Publius Popillius Laenas. Site of the Lapis Pollae milestone (CIL I2 638), a Republican-era inscription recording cumulative distances from here to Nuceria, Capua, Muranum, Cosentia, Valentia and Regium — the single best source for the road's overall shape.

properties.name: Nerulum
properties.notes: An ancient Lucanian town taken by Rome in 317 BCE (Livy). Modern identification is contested between Rotonda and Lagonegro; the Barrington Atlas favors Rotonda, used here.

properties.name: Muranum
properties.notes: Modern Morano Calabro. Fixed both by the Antonine Itinerary (14 Roman miles from Nerulum) and independently by the Lapis Pollae (74 miles from Forum Popilii) — a rare case where two ancient sources agree.

properties.name: Caprasia
properties.notes: Near modern Castrovillari (contrada Ciparsia, which preserves the name). Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography places it on this stretch, roughly 28 miles from Consentia, though its exact position relative to the next station wasn't confirmable enough to attach that figure here.
sources: Smith's Dictionary of Greek and Roman Geography, s.v. Consentia (via search)

properties.name: Interamnium
properties.notes: Modern San Lorenzo del Vallo — the name means "between two rivers," describing its position between the Crati's tributaries on the way down to Consentia.
sources: Digital Atlas of the Roman Empire (DARE), imperium.ahlfeldt.se/places/22548.html

properties.name: Consentia
properties.notes: Modern Cosenza, capital of the Bruttii — the Lapis Pollae places it 123 Roman miles from Forum Popilii, a major waypoint on the road's long southern leg.

properties.name: Ad Fluvium Sabatum
properties.notes: A river-crossing station where the road forded the Savuto, in the Savuto-Reventino area. The exact ford location is still debated in the modern archaeological literature and has never been pinned to one excavated spot.
sources: Roberto Spadea et al., "La via Regio-Capuam nell'area del Savuto-Reventino," academia.edu/39901904

properties.name: Ad Turres
properties.notes: Modern Sambiase, now part of Lamezia Terme, named for a pair of Roman watchtowers that once stood here. The station also appears on the Tabula Peutingeriana.

properties.name: Vibo Valentia
properties.notes: A Latin colony founded in 192 BCE on the site of the Greek city of Hipponion. The Antonine Itinerary's mileage from Ad Turres to here does not clear a straight-line sanity check against these two towns' real coordinates, so no figure is claimed for this leg.

properties.name: Nicotera
properties.notes: One of the few stations on this road to keep its ancient name essentially unchanged into the modern town.

properties.name: Ad Mallias
properties.notes: Modern Bagnara Calabra, on the coast road running down toward the Strait of Messina crossing.

properties.name: Columna
properties.notes: "Columna Rhegia," a marker station near modern Cannitello at the narrowest ferry crossing to Sicily — the site was never definitively excavated, so several nearby candidate points have been proposed.
sources: Local Calabrian antiquarian sources (via search); site position approximate

properties.name: Regium
properties.notes: Modern Reggio Calabria, the road's terminus at the Strait of Messina — the closest crossing point to Sicily and the end of a road that ran the full length of the Italian peninsula's toe.

properties.name: Gabii
properties.notes: An old Latin League city 12 Roman miles from Rome — the road out to it was originally called Via Gabina before its later extension to Praeneste gave the whole route its familiar name.

properties.name: Ad Quintanas
properties.notes: Took its name from colonists of Labicum settled on land divided into quintana plots, per Livy. Location approximate along the known route rather than a pinned excavated point.

properties.name: Ad Statuas
properties.notes: Near modern San Cesareo, named for a profusion of decorative statuary and the point where the road forked toward Tusculum, Praeneste and Gabii. A cistern faced in Severan-era brickwork survives nearby. The Itinerary's claimed 3 mp from Ad Quintanas doesn't clear a straight-line sanity check against these two sites' real coordinates, so no distance figure is claimed for this leg.
sources: Nibby, Analisi storico-topografica-antiquaria della carta de' dintorni di Roma

properties.name: Ad Pictas
properties.notes: Located near Valle Fredda in Valmontone's territory by a 2013 scholarly study identifying the Via Labicana's route through this stretch.
sources: "The Via Latina, the Via Labicana and the location of Ad Pictas," Papers of the British School at Rome (2013)

properties.name: Ad Bivium
properties.notes: "At the fork" — the Tabula Peutingeriana's largest Via Labicana station, 30 Roman miles from Rome, where the road split toward the Via Latina. The catacomb of Sant'Ilario was excavated on the same site.
sources: Rivista di Archeologia Cristiana 99 (2023), on the Ad Bivium excavation

properties.name: Ficulea
properties.notes: An old Latin League town that gave the road its original name, Via Ficulensis, before it was extended to Nomentum. Its precise site remains debated among 19th-century and modern topographers alike; no Roman-mile figure for the distance from Rome could be sourced with confidence.

properties.name: Compitum Anagninum
properties.notes: Excavated 2007-08 at Osteria della Fontana below Anagni, revealing a Temple of Diana and a structure nicknamed the "Circo Marittimo" beside a since-vanished sacred lake. The point where the Via Latina, Via Labicana and the Praenestina's extension physically converge in the Sacco valley.
sources: anagnia.com, Osteria della Fontana excavation reports

properties.name: Ferentinum
properties.notes: Modern Ferentino, a Hernician hill town on the Via Latina's climb through the Sacco valley.

properties.name: Frusino
properties.notes: Modern Frosinone, another Hernician town absorbed early into Rome's road network.

properties.name: Fregellanum
properties.notes: Fregellae, a major Latin colony founded in 328 BCE, was destroyed by Rome in 125 BCE after leading a revolt. Its road station lived on afterward under the diminished name Fregellanum, across the Liri from its replacement colony, Fabrateria Nova.

properties.name: Fabrateria Nova
properties.notes: Founded to resettle Fregellae's survivors after Rome razed their city in 125 BCE, sited just across the Liri river from the ruins. Distinct from the older, separate town of Fabrateria Vetus near modern Ceccano, off this stretch of road.

properties.name: Aquinum
properties.notes: Modern Aquino, birthplace of the satirist Juvenal, with a substantial surviving amphitheater and forum. The Itinerary's claimed 8 mp from Fabrateria Nova doesn't clear a straight-line sanity check against these two towns' real coordinates, so no distance figure is claimed for this leg.

properties.name: Casinum
properties.notes: Modern Cassino. Ummidia Quadratilla, a wealthy local benefactor, funded the town's surviving amphitheater and theater.

properties.name: Venafrum
properties.notes: Modern Venafro, renowned in antiquity for the quality of its olive oil — Cato and Varro both praised Venafran oil as the best in Italy.

properties.name: Teanum Sidicinum
properties.notes: Modern Teano, capital of the Sidicini before Rome absorbed the town — a major road junction where this Beneventum-bound branch of the Via Latina met the route continuing on to Casilinum and the Via Appia near Capua.

properties.name: Alifae
properties.notes: Modern Alife, an old Samnite town on the road's final stretch toward Beneventum.

properties.name: Telesia
properties.notes: Near modern San Salvatore Telesino, the last stop before Beneventum on this branch of the Via Latina.

properties.name: Rutupiae
properties.notes: The main Roman gateway into Britain — modern Richborough, Kent. Founded as the beachhead for the 43 CE invasion, it grew into a fortified supply port with its own monumental arch, and every legion, official and letter crossing the Channel to the province passed through here.

properties.name: Durovernum Cantiacorum
properties.notes: Modern Canterbury, Kent — a civitas capital of the Cantiaci on the direct road between Londinium and the Channel port at Rutupiae. Excavations have found a Roman theatre and public baths beneath the later medieval city.

properties.name: Durolevum
properties.notes: A staging post the Antonine Itinerary places between Durobrivae and Durovernum, but archaeologists still disagree on its exact site — candidates cluster around Ospringe and Syndale near modern Faversham.

properties.name: Durobrivae
properties.notes: Modern Rochester, Kent, where Watling Street crossed the tidal River Medway. A bridge here carried the road since at least the 1st century CE, and the crossing gave the town its name — durobrivae means roughly 'fort by the bridges.'

properties.name: Sulloniacis
properties.notes: A staging post at Brockley Hill, Stanmore, on the ridge northwest of Londinium — excavation has turned up large-scale pottery kilns here supplying the capital with tableware.

properties.name: Verulamium
properties.notes: Modern St Albans, one of only three Romano-British towns granted the high status of municipium. It was sacked and burned during Boudica's revolt in 60/61 CE, then rebuilt with a forum, basilica and theatre — thriving again well before Trajan's reign.

properties.name: Durocobrivis
properties.notes: A mansio at modern Dunstable, Bedfordshire, where Watling Street crosses the prehistoric Icknield Way — a road junction of real strategic value, not just a rest stop.

properties.name: Magiovinium
properties.notes: A walled way-station near modern Fenny Stratford, Milton Keynes, where excavation has recovered a defended enclosure alongside the road plus a scatter of Roman-period burials in the surrounding fields.

properties.name: Lactodurum
properties.notes: Modern Towcester, Northamptonshire — a defended small town that grew up around its Watling Street mansio, with a ditched enclosure still traceable in the town's later medieval street plan.

properties.name: Bannaventa
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at Whilton Lodge, Northamptonshire, that grew into a proper small town with its own defenses by the later Roman period — one of several Watling Street vici that outgrew their original function as a simple stopping point.

properties.name: Tripontium
properties.notes: A mansio at Cave's Inn, Shawell, Warwickshire, named for the three bridges that once carried the road over the River Avon and its side channels here.

properties.name: Venonis
properties.notes: The junction at High Cross, Leicestershire, where Watling Street crosses the Fosse Way — the two great cross-country roads of Roman Britain meeting at a single point, making this one of the busiest crossroads in the province.

properties.name: Manduessedum
properties.notes: Modern Mancetter, Warwickshire — a mansio and small fort site, traditionally linked by local tradition (though not firmly proven) to the general area of Boudica's last battle against Rome in 60/61 CE.

properties.name: Letocetum
properties.notes: Modern Wall, Staffordshire — one of the best-excavated mansiones in Britain, with a substantial bathhouse and guest inn still standing to window height, run for travelers and imperial couriers on the road.

properties.name: Pennocrucium
properties.notes: A mansio at Water Eaton, Staffordshire, where Watling Street crossed a tributary of the River Penk — the name itself is Brittonic for roughly 'chief crossing.'

properties.name: Uxacona
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at Redhill, Shropshire, on the final stretch of Watling Street before it reached Viroconium — one of the lesser-excavated stations on this road, known mainly from itinerary sources.

properties.name: Viroconium Cornoviorum
properties.notes: Modern Wroxeter, Shropshire — Watling Street's northwestern terminus and, by the early 2nd century, the fourth-largest city in Roman Britain, civitas capital of the Cornovii with a monumental forum and one of the largest known Roman bathhouses in the province.

properties.name: Isca Dumnoniorum
properties.notes: Modern Exeter, Devon — the Fosse Way's southwestern terminus and civitas capital of the Dumnonii, built over an earlier legionary fortress once garrisoned by Legio II Augusta.

properties.name: Lindinis
properties.notes: Modern Ilchester, Somerset — a mansio that later grew important enough to become the seat of its own civitas, the Durotriges Lendinienses, splitting administrative duties with Dorchester.

properties.name: Aquae Sulis
properties.notes: Modern Bath, Somerset, where the Fosse Way met a natural hot spring sacred to the Romano-Celtic goddess Sulis Minerva — already, by Trajan's reign, drawing pilgrims and invalids to its temple and bathing complex.

properties.name: Corinium Dobunnorum
properties.notes: Modern Cirencester, Gloucestershire — civitas capital of the Dobunni and, by the later Roman period, the second-largest town in Britain after Londinium, sitting at the crossing of the Fosse Way and Ermin Street.

properties.name: Ratae Corieltauvorum
properties.notes: Modern Leicester — civitas capital of the Corieltauvi, with a forum-basilica complex and public baths whose Jewry Wall still stands among the tallest surviving Roman masonry in Britain.

properties.name: Vernemetum
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at Willoughby-on-the-Wolds, Nottinghamshire, whose Brittonic name means 'great sacred grove' — a shared node linking the Fosse Way toward the Ermine Street corridor further east.

properties.name: Margidunum
properties.notes: A defended way-station at East Bridgford/Bingham, Nottinghamshire, with its own ditched fortification — the Fosse Way here ran close enough to hostile territory in the early conquest period to need real defenses, not just an open mansio.

properties.name: Ad Pontem
properties.notes: A fort and way-station at East Stoke, Nottinghamshire, guarding the Fosse Way's crossing of the River Trent — its very name simply means 'at the bridge.'

properties.name: Crococalana
properties.notes: A mansio near Brough, Nottinghamshire, the last stop on the Fosse Way before it met the Ermine Street corridor and the colonia at Lindum — a genuine road junction as well as a rest station.

properties.name: Corstopitum
properties.notes: Modern Corbridge, Northumberland — the Stanegate's eastern anchor and one of the largest fort-and-supply-base sites on the northern frontier, where the Stanegate met Dere Street running up from York. Granaries built here to provision Trajan's northern garrisons still stand.

properties.name: Newbrough
properties.notes: A small fortlet on the Stanegate west of Corbridge, under an acre in size — one of the modest garrison posts strung along this pre-Wall frontier road roughly every few miles.

properties.name: Haltwhistle Burn
properties.notes: A small fortlet above the Haltwhistle Burn in Northumberland, part of the same close-set chain of minor posts along the Stanegate that would later inform the spacing of milecastles on Hadrian's Wall.

properties.name: Magnis
properties.notes: The fort at Carvoran, Northumberland, guarding the point where the Stanegate crosses the Maiden Way running north from the Pennines — a genuine road-junction garrison, not just a way-station.

properties.name: Nether Denton
properties.notes: A fort and attached civilian vicus at Nether Denton, Cumbria, on the Stanegate's approach to the Irthing valley — one of the string of garrisons holding this frontier road two decades before Hadrian's Wall existed.

properties.name: Boothby
properties.notes: A small fortlet near Brampton, Cumbria, sized for a handful of soldiers rather than a full garrison — a change-of-horses post rather than a fighting position.

properties.name: Brampton Old Church
properties.notes: A fort controlling the Stanegate's crossing of the River Irthing near Brampton, Cumbria — command of this river crossing made it one of the more substantial posts on the road's western stretch.

properties.name: Luguvalium
