properties.notes: Modern Carlisle, Cumbria — the Stanegate's western terminus and, within a few years of Trajan's death, capital of the whole northern frontier zone. A fort had stood here since the Flavian conquest of the north, decades before Hadrian's Wall was ever planned.

properties.name: Eboracum
properties.notes: Modern York — headquarters fortress of Legio IX Hispana and then Legio VI Victrix, and Ermine Street's northern terminus. By 117 CE it was already the military and administrative center of the whole northern frontier.

properties.name: Petuaria
properties.notes: Modern Brough-on-Humber, East Yorkshire — a civitas center for the Parisi and a Humber-crossing point, on an alternate branch of the road network linking Eboracum toward Lincoln.

properties.name: Legeolium
properties.notes: A fort and mansio at modern Castleford, West Yorkshire, where Ermine Street crossed the River Aire — the fort guarded the crossing while the mansio served travelers on the York-Lincoln road.

properties.name: Danum
properties.notes: Modern Doncaster, South Yorkshire — a fort and mansio on Ermine Street's crossing of the River Don, part of the chain of garrisons securing the road between York and Lincoln.

properties.name: Segelocum
properties.notes: A mansio at Littleborough, Nottinghamshire, where Ermine Street forded the River Trent — the crossing itself, more than any settlement, is what put a station here.

properties.name: Lindum Colonia
properties.notes: Modern Lincoln — a legionary fortress converted into a colonia for army veterans, and the meeting point of Ermine Street with the Fosse Way running southwest toward Exeter. One of only four such veteran coloniae in Roman Britain.

properties.name: Ad Savonem (Safo fl.)
properties.notes: The Tabula Peutingeriana marks the Via Domitiana's crossing of the river Savo only as "Safo fl." (the river itself), about 7 Roman miles south of Sinuessa — a different crossing from the well-known Pons Campanus, which carries the inland Via Appia over the same river near Casilinum. No bridge structure or exact ford has been pinpointed archaeologically for this crossing; the point given here is an approximate placement near the modern Savone river mouth.
sources: Tabula Peutingeriana, Segment VI (K. Miller, Itineraria Romana, entry 347, "Safo fl.")
Statius, Silvae 4.3 (river-crossing context of the road)

properties.name: Pons Vulturni (bridge over the Volturnus)
properties.notes: The Via Domitiana's centerpiece engineering feat, a bridge over the Volturnus near its mouth that Statius personifies and celebrates at length — the river-god Vulturnus boasts of finally "carrying a bridge" instead of scattering into marshy fords, a passage written to mark the road's 95 CE dedication. The adjoining Roman colonia of Volturnum (founded 194 BCE) grew up beside the crossing; masonry from the Roman bridge was later reused as the base of the medieval Castel Volturno fortress on the same spot.

properties.name: Liternum
properties.notes: A Roman colonia founded in 194 BCE on the coastal plain between the Volturnus mouth and Cumae, which the new Via Domitiana ran directly through in 95 CE. Scipio Africanus retired here after his political fall and was buried nearby, a detail Seneca later used the town to reflect on — giving the road's route through Liternum a literary weight beyond its role as a waystation.

properties.name: In Vineis
properties.notes: A minor waystation — the name means "among the vineyards" — recorded on the Tabula Peutingeriana between Cumae and Puteoli, generally identified with the site of Arco Felice, where Domitian's engineers cut a dramatic passage through the hill of Monte Grillo to carry the road toward Puteoli. The still-standing arch there (Arco Felice Vecchio, roughly 20m tall) is one of the road's clearest surviving monuments.
sources: Tabula Peutingeriana, Segment VI (K. Miller, Itineraria Romana)
archeoflegrei.it, "I Campi Flegrei nella Tabula Peutingeriana"

properties.name: Antiochia Caesarea
properties.notes: The caput viae — every milestone on the Via Sebaste counted its distance from this Augustan colony. Refounded as a Roman veteran settlement and used as the region's main garrison and administrative base, Antioch anchored the road the governor Cornutus Arruntius Aquila built in 6 BCE to move troops quickly against the Taurus hill tribes and down to the Pamphylian coast.

properties.name: Apollonia
properties.notes: A Hellenistic foundation in Pisidia (earlier called Mordiaeon) that the Via Sebaste's Augustan builders folded into the new road network as the first major stop southwest of Antioch, on the stretch that swung the route toward Lake Burdur and Comama. No individual milestone distance from Antioch survives for this stretch.

properties.name: Comama
properties.notes: An Augustan veteran colony (Colonia Iulia Augusta Prima Fida Comama), one of five planted around Antioch in 6 BCE to pin down the Pisidian mountain tribes. An Augustan milestone found on the site itself reads CXXII — 122 Roman miles from Antioch, the road's caput viae, which this figure reflects rather than a distance from Apollonia specifically. Here the road split: one branch ran west to Olbasa, another southeast to Cremna, and the mainline continued south through the Climax Pass to Perge.

properties.name: Olbasa
properties.notes: A western branch off the Via Sebaste at Comama, roughly 25-30 km away (no surviving milestone gives an exact figure). Another of Augustus's Pisidian veteran colonies, titled Colonia Iulia Augusta like its sister foundations, planted to extend Roman control and road access into the western highlands.

properties.name: Cremna
properties.notes: A southeastern branch off the Via Sebaste at Comama, roughly 35 km away (no surviving milestone gives an exact figure). Perched on a defensible plateau above the Cestrus river gorge, Cremna was garrisoned by Augustan veterans as a forward post against the Homonadensian tribes; a century after its founding it withstood a dramatic siege by the rebel Lydius against a Roman relief force, an episode Strabo records.

properties.name: Mansio in Klimax
properties.notes: The best-preserved Roman mansio in all of Asia Minor, still standing to roof height in the Doseme Bogazi pass with a courtyard, nine ground-floor rooms for pack animals and six upper rooms for travelers. An Augustan milestone beside it reads CXXXIX — 139 Roman miles from Antioch, 17 past Comama's own CXXII marker — fixing the mansio at the road's critical Taurus Mountains chokepoint between the Pisidian plateau and the Pamphylian coast. Coordinates are an approximate placement for the pass; no public exact figure was found for the mansio building itself.
sources: Mitchell, Wagner & Williams (2021), Roman Archaeology in a South Anatolian Landscape: The Via Sebaste, the Mansio in the Doseme Bogazi, and Regional Transhumance in Pamphylia and Pisidia, Koc University Press

properties.name: Perge
properties.notes: The Via Sebaste's Mediterranean end point, giving Rome's inland Pisidian colonies a direct paved route to a Pamphylian port. Acts 13 places Paul and Barnabas landing and later re-embarking here, almost certainly using this same road on their inland leg to Pisidian Antioch. A 2008 survey documented a newly-identified stretch of the road and its roadside buildings running from here up to the Climax Pass.

properties.name: Ad Sorores
properties.notes: First overnight halt heading north out of Emerita Augusta on the road to Asturica, roughly where the modern village of Casas de Don Antonio now stands.

properties.name: Castra Caecilia
properties.notes: A former Republican-era army camp on the Ribera del Marco springs, later a road station serving the site that grew into modern Caceres.

properties.name: Turmulus
properties.notes: Marked the crossing of the Tagus at Alconetar, where a Roman bridge carried the road over the river near modern Garrovillas de Alconetar.

properties.name: Rusticiana
properties.notes: A waystation on the plain north of the Tagus, generally placed at modern Galisteo, walled centuries later on the same defensible river bend.

properties.name: Capara
properties.notes: A full Roman town, not just a waystation, with its own forum, baths and an amphitheater. Its four-faced arch still stands astride the old road between Guijo de Granadilla and Oliva de Plasencia, the best-preserved monument on the entire route.
properties.image_credit: Arch of Caparra, Extremadura · Wikimedia Commons

properties.name: Caecilius Vicus
properties.notes: A roadside settlement at the southern foot of the mountain pass into the Duero basin, on the site of the hot springs at modern Banos de Montemayor.

properties.name: Ad Lippos
properties.notes: A short relay stage climbing through the Sierra de Bejar pass; no excavated remains confirm the exact spot, and the village of La Calzada de Bejar preserves only the road's name, not a proven station site.

properties.name: Sentice
properties.notes: The highest point of the whole road between Emerita and Asturica, somewhere in the hills around modern Fuenterroble de Salvatierra. Archaeologists are still searching for its exact footprint.

properties.name: Salmantica
properties.notes: A walled hilltop town on the Tormes, already old when Hannibal besieged it in 220 BCE. In 117 CE it is a working stop on the imperial road, not yet the university city its Roman bridge still carries traffic toward today.

properties.name: Sibarim
properties.notes: Recorded as sitting almost exactly halfway between Salmantica and Ocelo Duri, in open country north of Salamanca near modern Calzada de Valdunciel, but with no confirmed archaeological footprint.

properties.name: Ocelo Duri
properties.notes: Named for its position on the Duero, "the Eye of the Duero," near where the Romans defeated the Lusitanian leader Viriathus. Excavated road remains survive near modern Villalazan, Zamora.

properties.name: Albocela
properties.notes: A Vaccaei-territory station on the Duero's north bank, generally but not conclusively placed under modern Toro; distance here is estimated from the road's known path rather than a surviving itinerary figure.

properties.name: Amallobriga
properties.notes: A station on the open Tierra de Campos plain, tentatively placed near modern Tiedra though the identification is disputed among Spanish archaeologists; distance estimated from the road's known path.

properties.name: Brigaecium
properties.notes: An Astures-territory town on the last stretch before Asturica Augusta, independently recorded as 40 Roman miles from that city. Its remains sit at the Penon de Villabrazaro, near Benavente.

properties.name: Vodgoriacum
properties.notes: A vicus at modern Waudrez, near Binche, on the stretch of road running north out of Bavay toward Tongeren. Excavation has confirmed continuous Roman-period occupation here, matching the Antonine Itinerary's placement between Bagacum and Geminiacum.

properties.name: Geminiacum
properties.notes: One of the best-excavated vici on the whole Bavay-Cologne road, at Liberchies in modern Pont-a-Celles, dug systematically since 1956. Coin finds there run continuously through the Roman period, confirming it as a real working roadside settlement rather than a guess from the text alone.

properties.name: Perniciacum
properties.notes: A vicus at modern Braives, named Pernaco on the Peutinger Table and Perniciacum in the Antonine Itinerary, on the long stretch of road between Liberchies and Tongeren.

properties.name: Aduaca Tungrorum
properties.notes: Civitas capital of the Tungri, at modern Tongeren, the largest town on this stretch of Gallia Belgica and still ringed today by its Roman-era walls. The road crossed here on its way to the Rhine frontier.

properties.name: Coriovallum
properties.notes: A road-junction settlement at modern Heerlen, where this road met the north-south route linking the Rhine legionary bases. Excavated bathhouse remains are still on public display beneath the modern town center.

properties.name: Iuliacum
properties.notes: A vicus at modern Julich, the last waystation before the road reached the Rhine at Cologne. Its name survives almost unchanged into the modern German town.

properties.name: Colonia Agrippina
properties.notes: This branch's eastern terminus at the Rhine, modern Cologne, seat of the governor of Germania Inferior and home port of the Rhine fleet. The road tied Britannia's Channel crossing directly to this legionary frontier in one continuous line, closing out the Bavay-Cologne stretch of Via Agrippa's northern network.
